title: Tier I Capstone — Principled Eclecticism

points.h: There Is No Single Best Method
pts: Comparative method studies across decades have failed to prove any single method universally superior to the others.
This isn't a failure of research — it reflects that context, not method alone, determines what works.
Treat any claim of a single universally 'best' method with appropriate scepticism.

v: Cards with method names and short descriptions

items: Give pairs of teachers cards naming major methods, with a one-line description of each.
Place them on a timeline.
For each, note one thing it got right and one limitation.
Discuss: which ideas from each method still appear in your teaching?
Discuss Prabhu’s question: why is there no best method?
Each group demonstrates a two-minute sample of one method.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Grammar–translation: got right: attention to accuracy and to the first language. Limitation: little speaking.
Audiolingualism: got right: practice and pronunciation. Limitation: little meaning.
Communicative teaching: got right: meaningful use. Limitation: sometimes neglects accuracy.

blocks.x: Almost every method got something right. That is why a teacher can learn from all of them.

body: Purpose: to show methods as a history rather than a race. Content: a winding road with milestones labelled with method names and decades; the road ends not at a finish line but at a crossroads labelled ‘Your context’. Style: gentle, map-like. Board version: a timeline with arrows.

items: Canva (free for education) or Google Slides for a digital timeline.

blocks.x: Method cards on string across the room.

pts: Instead of adopting one method wholesale, draw principles from many — communicative, lexical, task-based — and apply them contextually.
Units 1–24 were never separate techniques to memorise in isolation; they are principles to combine as a given class demands.
Eclecticism here means principled selection, not directionless mixing.

items: List ten techniques you use (e.g. pair work, drilling, a lead-in, recasts).
For each, write the principle it serves.
Group the techniques by principle.
Notice which principles are well represented in your teaching, and which are rare.
Do the task with the unit titles from Part I as the list.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Pair work → maximize learner talk time.
Drilling → build automaticity.
Recasts → focus on form within meaning.
Lead-in → activate schemata.
Graded readers → large amounts of comprehensible input.

blocks.x: If you cannot name the principle behind a technique, ask whether you need it. If you can, you know when to use it and when to leave it out. That is the difference between principled eclecticism and simply mixing techniques.

body: Purpose: to show principles supporting techniques. Content: a tree whose roots are labelled with principles (input, output, interaction, noticing, affect, context) and whose branches carry leaves labelled with techniques. Style: organic, warm. Board version: a simple tree drawing.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a two-column principle and technique table.

blocks.x: A two-column table in the teaching journal.

pts: The right teaching choice depends on this specific class and context, not a general theory divorced from the room.
Unit 2's needs analysis and Unit 15's differentiation are both expressions of this same particularity principle.
A technique that worked brilliantly with one class is a hypothesis for the next one, not a guarantee.

v: A class list; notes from earlier needs analysis (Unit 2)

items: For one class, write a short profile: age, level, languages spoken, interests, resources, timetable, exam pressures.
Note three features that make this class different from others you teach.
For each feature, note one teaching decision it should affect.
Review after a month: did the decisions work?
Compare profiles of two classes of the same grade.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Class 7B: 46 learners, mostly Kannada and Urdu speakers, some Telugu. Very keen on cricket and mobile games. Little English at home. One functioning projector shared with two classes. Board exam not until Class 10.
Use cricket and gaming themes for reading.
Allow home-language brainstorming before English output.
Plan board-based lessons; the projector is a bonus, not a basis.

body: Purpose: to show particularity. Content: a magnifying glass over one classroom among many on a map, revealing details inside (learners’ faces, a cricket bat, a blackboard, a language chart). Style: detailed but friendly. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free) for a learner questionnaire.

pts: A technique that's theoretically ideal but unusable in your real teaching context isn't actually a good choice for it.
Unit 17's large-class adaptations and Unit 18's technology limits are both practicality checks in this sense.
Theory informs the choice; practicality determines whether the choice survives an actual lesson.

v: A new technique or idea from training

items: Choose an idea you have met in training or reading.
Test it against five practical questions (see model language).
Adapt it until it passes, or set it aside.
Try it, then note what happened.
Share adapted ideas at a staff meeting or teacher circle.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Does it fit the time I have?
Does it fit the space and class size?
Does it need resources I do not have?
Will learners understand what to do?
Can I manage it alone?

blocks.x: An example: a gallery walk in a class of fifty with fixed benches fails question 2. Adapted version: posters are passed from bench to bench instead. Kumaravadivelu’s idea of practicality also means that teachers generate theory from their own practice, not only apply others’ theory.

body: Purpose: to show practicality as a filter. Content: a large, elaborate idea (a cloud with many parts) passing through a funnel labelled ‘Time, space, resources, learners’, and coming out as a smaller, sturdy version that fits into a real classroom. Style: playful. Board version: a funnel drawing.

items: A notes app for recording what happened.

pts: Teaching is shaped by learners' social, cultural and political realities, not just their linguistic ones.
Units 23 and 24 — inclusive teaching and intercultural competence — are both expressions of this wider possibility parameter.
Ignoring these realities doesn't make a method more neutral; it just makes its assumptions invisible.

items: Look at your class profile.
Ask: what social, economic or cultural realities shape these learners’ experience of English?
Consider access: who has devices, books or English at home, and who does not?
Consider identity: whose languages and cultures are visible in the classroom?
Decide on one change that widens what is possible for learners with the least access.
Discuss with colleagues how English affects learners’ future opportunities in your area.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Few learners have English at home → set homework that needs no English-speaking adult.
Some learners feel their home language is not valued → use it deliberately in class (Unit 5).
Some girls leave school early → include texts and role models showing women in varied careers.

blocks.x: English in India can open doors, and it can also divide. Kumaravadivelu’s possibility parameter asks teachers to recognize this and to teach in ways that widen, not narrow, learners’ choices. Units 23 and 24 are applications of this principle.

body: Purpose: to show possibility. Content: a corridor of doors, some open with light streaming in, others closed; learners walking towards them, and a teacher holding one open. Style: hopeful. Board version: not applicable.

items: None needed; this is a reflection task.

body: Prabhu’s Communicational Teaching Project in South India (1979–84) was one of the earliest large-scale trials of what became known as task-based teaching. Learners worked on problem-solving tasks such as reading timetables and maps, with attention on meaning rather than on a grammar syllabus (Prabhu 1987). Part II of this book returns to task-based teaching in detail.

pts: Articulate, even briefly, the principles that now guide your own eclectic practice.
This series has supplied the vocabulary and the toolkit; the synthesis into a personal philosophy is the teacher's own work.
A stated philosophy, revisited periodically, keeps eclectic practice principled rather than merely inconsistent.

items: Complete these sentences: I believe learners learn English best when… Therefore, in my classes, I… I pay special attention to… I am still learning how to…
Combine the sentences into a paragraph of about 150 words.
Share it with a colleague and ask: ‘Would I see this if I observed your class?’
Keep it in your teaching journal.
Revisit and revise it at the end of each term.
Create a visual version: a mind map or a drawing.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: I believe learners learn English best when they use it for real purposes in a classroom where mistakes are welcome. Therefore, in my classes, I plan tasks that need communication, and I give learners time to prepare before they speak. I use learners’ home languages as a bridge, not a barrier. I pay special attention to learners who are quiet, and to the ones who find reading hard. I am still learning how to give useful feedback on writing to a class of fifty.

body: Purpose: to show a teaching philosophy as a guide. Content: a compass with four points labelled with a teacher’s key beliefs (e.g. ‘Meaning first’, ‘Every language counts’, ‘Safe to try’, ‘Practice matters’). Style: elegant, personal. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free) for a document that can be revised each term.

blocks.x: The first page of the teaching journal.

points.h: From Tier I to Tier II
pts: Foundations equipped the single lesson (Units 1–10) and the single unit and course (Units 11–20), then the wider classroom and learner context (Units 21–24).
Tier II assumes all of this is in place and turns to fully integrating the skills through task-based, fluency-focused methodology.
Nothing in Tier II replaces these foundations — it builds directly on top of them.

items: Read the list of Part I units.
Mark each unit: ✓ = I use this confidently; ~ = I use this sometimes; ? = I need to work on this.
Choose two ‘?’ units to focus on next term.
Read the list of Part II units and note which ones connect to your chosen focus.
A teacher circle creates a shared development plan.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Units 1–10: the single lesson (needs, the four skills, sounds, vocabulary, grammar, classroom craft, feedback, planning).
Units 11–20: the unit and the course (syllabus, coursebook, scheme of work, mixed ability, age, large classes, technology, homework).
Units 21–24: the wider classroom (assessment, affect, inclusion, culture).

blocks.x: Part II builds on these to integrate the skills through tasks and fluency-focused teaching.

Content: a building cross-section; the foundation is labelled ‘Part I: Foundations’ with small bricks naming key units; above, a floor under construction is labelled ‘Part II: Skill Integration’. Style: architectural, clear. Board version: a simple building outline.

pts: Units 1 through 24 built a toolkit; this poster is the reminder that the toolkit exists to serve informed judgement, not to replace it.
No poster in this series was ever meant to be applied mechanically, independent of the class in front of you.
Tier II begins from here — deeper methodology, same underlying principle of principled, context-driven choice.

items: Choose one technique from Part I you used with success.
Describe one class where it might not work, and why.
Describe how you would adapt it for that class.
Share with a colleague.
Write a short case study of a lesson in which you departed from your plan for good reasons.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Technique: think–pair–share. Worked well with Class 8, who enjoy talking. Might not work with Class 6A, where learners are very new to English and pairs fall silent. Adaptation: give a sentence frame and a picture prompt; allow the ‘pair’ stage in the home language, then share in English.

blocks.x: No unit in this book gives you a script. Each gives you a tool and a principle. The judgement about when and how to use them is yours.

body: Purpose: to close Part I. Content: an open toolbox containing small labelled tools (e.g. ‘lead-in’, ‘concept check’, ‘pair work’, ‘graded reader’), with a hand choosing one tool while the teacher looks at a class. Style: warm, final. Board version: not applicable.

items: None needed; this is a reflection task.

body: Write your teaching philosophy (point 6) this week. Put it away. Take it out at the end of the year, after you have worked through Part II, and see what has changed.

dek: Unit 25 of 100: no single method has ever proven universally best. This capstone closes Foundations by turning twenty-four posters of tools into a working teaching philosophy.

aims.x: This unit closes Part I. It pulls together the previous twenty-four units and asks how a teacher chooses among them. The answer offered is principled eclecticism: selecting and combining techniques for good reasons, in response to a particular class.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why no single method has been proven best;
distinguish principled eclecticism from random mixing;
apply Kumaravadivelu’s parameters of particularity, practicality and possibility to your own teaching;
write a short statement of your teaching philosophy;
see how Part I prepares for Part II.

why: Why this matters. Foundations was never meant to hand over one fixed method. It was meant to build the judgement to choose, combine and adapt — which is the actual, permanent skill.

background.x: The history of language teaching is often told as a sequence of methods: grammar–translation, the direct method, audiolingualism, the silent way, suggestopedia, communicative language teaching, task-based teaching. Each was promoted, at some point, as the answer. Large studies in the 1960s set out to prove which method worked best, and found no clear winner. In 1990, N. S. Prabhu, whose work in Bangalore on the Communicational Teaching Project influenced task-based teaching worldwide, published an article with a memorable title: ‘There is no best method—why?’ (Prabhu 1990). His answer was that what matters most is the teacher’s sense of plausibility: a teacher’s own developing understanding of how learning happens, which guides their decisions in the classroom.

B. Kumaravadivelu (1994, 2003, 2006) took this further. He described a postmethod condition, in which teachers stop searching for the best method and instead develop their own practice from principles. He proposed three parameters to guide this practice. Particularity means teaching that is sensitive to the particular group of teachers and learners in a particular context. Practicality means teachers theorize from their practice and practise what they theorize. Possibility means recognizing the social, political and cultural realities that shape learners’ lives and identities.

These ideas fit Indian classrooms well. The same textbook is used by a teacher in a well-resourced city school and a teacher in a single-room rural school. No single method will work identically in both. Both the NEP 2020 and the NCF 2023 encourage teacher autonomy in choosing pedagogy (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). This unit gives you tools for using that autonomy well. Most of its activities are for you, the teacher.

items: Philosophy statement. A short written statement, reviewed by a peer for coherence and link to practice.
Adapted lesson. A lesson plan with notes explaining each choice by particularity, practicality or possibility.
Self-assessment. The Part I checklist, repeated at the end of the year.
Observation. A peer observes a lesson and notes which principles they see in practice.
Which method did you learn to teach in? What do you still use from it?
Can you name the principle behind each technique you use most often?
What makes your class particular?
Which good idea have you dropped because it was not practical? Could it be adapted?
What would widen the possibilities for the learners with least access in your class?
How has your view of teaching changed during Part I?

terms.def: Prabhu’s project in South India (1979–84), in which school classes learned English through problem-solving tasks rather than a grammatical syllabus; one of the earliest large-scale trials of task-based teaching (Prabhu 1987).

A defined set of classroom procedures based on a particular view of language and learning, such as the Audiolingual Method or the Direct Method; no single method has been shown to be best for all contexts.
In Kumaravadivelu’s (2001) postmethod pedagogy, the principle that teaching must be sensitive to a particular group of teachers and learners in a particular institutional and social context.
In Kumaravadivelu’s (2001) postmethod pedagogy, the principle that teaching should draw on learners’ sociopolitical awareness and identity, and aim at social change as well as language learning.
Kumaravadivelu’s (1994) term for the situation in which teachers look for an alternative to method rather than an alternative method, building their own principled practice.

1. In assessment, whether a test is feasible given time, cost and resources. 2. In Kumaravadivelu’s (2001) postmethod pedagogy, the principle that teachers should theorize from their practice and practise what they theorize.
Combining techniques from different methods on the basis of a coherent rationale suited to the context, rather than mixing them at random.

A teacher’s own developing understanding of how learning happens, which guides classroom decisions (Prabhu 1990). Prabhu argued it matters more than any one method, and that it stays alive through reflection and engagement with ideas.
A teacher’s personal, reasoned set of beliefs about how languages are learned and how best to teach them, which guides classroom decisions and develops with experience and reflection.
